title: A compact six-beam 3D magneto-optical trap based on multifunctional metasurface chips
authors: Chen Qing, Huijie Sun, Yize Liu, Yuxuan Liao, Yongzhuo Li, Dengke Zhang, Xue Feng, Yidong Huang
abstract: Magneto-optical traps (MOTs), indispensable to cold-atom-based quantum computing and quantum precision measurement, are increasingly desired in compact and stable form. Particularly, the six-beam 3D-MOT, distinguished by symmetric geometry and superior trapping performance, finds particularly broad applications. Conventional implementations, however, rely on complex and bulky free-space optics, hindering miniaturization, practical assembly, and long-term stability. Here, we demonstrate a compact six-beam 3D-MOT system that employs two multifunctional optical metasurface chips to implement the optical-field functionalities required for cooling and trapping atoms. By combining two metasurface chips and a vacuum cell, a photonic-integrated cell module (PICM) is implemented as the core assembly and the volume is only" 73*73*107 mm^3" . In success, 1.3 * 10^3 Rb atoms are trapped and cooled to the temperature of ~183 μK. It should be noticed that the laser beam is guided to the metasurface through optical fiber, thus such fully fiber-coupled architecture enables straightforward and stable operations. We believe that this work would pave a practical route toward compact and portable 3D-MOT.
summary: The paper presents a breakthrough in miniaturizing the six-beam 3D Magneto-Optical Trap (MOT) by integrating all necessary beam manipulation optics onto multifunctional metasurface chips. This photonic-integrated module achieves high performance, trapping and cooling $	ext{}^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms to $183 \mu	ext{K}$ in a compact, fiber-coupled package. This development paves a practical route toward portable quantum sensing and computing platforms.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is developing a compact and stable implementation of the six-beam 3D Magneto-Optical Trap (MOT) to overcome the bulkiness of conventional free-space optics.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a compact, fiber-coupled 3D-MOT using metasurface chips, achieving trapping and cooling of $	ext{}^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms to a temperature of $\sim 183 \mu	ext{K}$.
method: The system integrates beam manipulation functions—including polarization conversion, beam deflection, and beam expansion—onto multifunctional metasurface chips fabricated using $\alpha$-Si on $	ext{SiO}_2$.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a Photonic-Integrated Cell Module (PICM) containing two metasurface chips within a hexagonal-prism vacuum cell. The MOT utilizes a quadrupole magnetic field generated by anti-Helmholtz coils.
key_observables: Trapped atom number ($>10^6$ atoms), temperature ($\sim 183 \mu	ext{K}$), polarization states (RCP/LCP), and beam deflection/expansion characteristics.
important_parameters: Metasurface geometry (e.g., $\alpha$-Si meta-atoms on $	ext{SiO}_2$), MOT volume ($73 	imes 73 	imes 10^7 	ext{ mm}^3$), and magnetic field gradient ($\sim 15 	ext{ G/cm}$).
main_assumptions: The system relies on the high refractive-index contrast between $\alpha$-Si and $	ext{SiO}_2$ for efficient lightwave manipulation, and the approach is claimed to be compatible with high-volume production.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the six-beam 3D-MOT, the layout of the core assembly, and details of the metasurface chip unit, showing the integration of optical functions.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity for miniaturization, presents the metasurface design (using inverse design and FDTD simulations), describes the fabrication process (EBL/ICP-RIE), and concludes with the experimental demonstration of the MOT performance.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of quantum optics by replacing bulky free-space optics with integrated photonic components, enabling portable and stable quantum measurement tools.

The system comprises two fiberized micro-lens arrays (FMLAs), two metasurface chips (MS chips), six compact mirrors, a regular hexagonal-prism vacuum cell, and anti-Helmholtz coils. Light from each FMLA illuminates its corresponding metasurface chip, which simultaneously performs polarization conversion, beam deflection, and beam expansion. The six resulting beams are reflected by the mirrors and converge at the cell center, forming three counter-propagating beam pairs in a rotationally symmetric configuration.
